newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian shares claw back ground as politics rumble.
newsitem.headline: Indian shares claw back ground as politics rumble.

text.p: Indian equity markets on Wednesday continued to claw back ground lost in the aftershock of the Congress party's move to oust Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's minority government.
Growing confidence that Finance Minister P. Chidambaram's widely acclaimed investor-friendly budget will be salvaged out of the political mess shone through the gloom, dealers said.
The government has said that it wants to pass the 1997/98 (April-March) budget, which was presented on February 28, before it faces a confidence vote on April 11.
Bombay's benchmark index climbed two percent on Tuesday, and and in early afternoon trading on Wednesday it had added almost another two percent.
The 30-share index was up 66.52, 1.94 percent at 3493.55 points at 1330 local (0800 GMT).

"What has emerged...is that there is a broad consensus amongst all political parties that it was a good budget and all efforts must be made to pass the budget," Tushar Sarda, president and chief executive at Daewoo told Reuters Financial Television on Wednesday.

Tampering with proposed corporate and personal tax cuts would alienate both the business community and middle income voters, which no party will want when chances for mid-term polls were so high, analysts said.

The Bharatiya Janatha Party, the single largest group in parliament, said the budget could be passed only after the confidence vote was first considered by parliament. The Congress said it might seek unspecified changes before approving the budget.
"All politicians seem to believe that it would be political suicide to oppose the budget," said a trader at a foreign institutional investor.
But he said the market's optimism should be laced with caution while the government's fate was in the balance.

Regardless of whether the government survives or falls, India is in for a lengthy period of political uncertainty, which will retard the economy, said Alok Sethi, director of NatWest Markets in Bombay.
"Sooner or later there will be a mid-term poll, and the fear will always be there," Sethi said.
And he said there should be no rush to buy into India.
"The window of opportunity for investors to buy shares is going to be long and wide. This market is not going to run away," Sethi said.

A trader at a foreign broking firm said the market started climbing on Tuesday because of hopes that the budget would go through. "That's uppermost on the market's mind." That was still a long way off Friday's 3663.53, the BSE index's last close before Congress withdrew vital support for the government on Sunday. The move chopped more than eight percent off the index on Monday to register its fourth largest decline ever.
The National Stock Exchange top 50 index was up 21.7 points, 2.24 percent, at 991.85 in afternoon trade.
The Delhi index also registered a continued recovery on Wednesday, gaining 8.11 points, 1.12 percent, to reach 733.59 in the first half hour of trading Wednesday.
